utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I understand that was marked for identification. It will be now an exhibit. Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in. Am I right if I say that this witness has face distortion but not voice distortion, and a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I would like to read a brief summary of the 92 ter statement. It shouldn't take more than five minutes. I expect that's about as much time as I will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If that is really a summary, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it is. Let me begin. The witness was a survivor or is a survivor of an execution of over a thousand Bosnian Muslim men and boys by VRS and MUP forces which took place at the Kravica warehouse on 13 July 1995. On 11 July 1995, the witness was forced to abandon his home in Srebrenica, where he had lived all his life. As the town and surrounding villages fell, the witness had to separate from his wife and two daughters near the village of Ravne Njive. While they fled to Potocari, the witness made his way towards Jaglici, where he learned a gathering of all the men would take place in order to go through the woods to Tuzla. The witness recalled that his brother and nephew who decided to go to Potocari did not survive. The witness arrived at Jaglici that evening, he spent the night there, and on the 12th, set out from there for Buljim, where he encountered the first of two ambushes in which many men were killed. When night fell, the witness and his group of six or seven along with many others were again ambushed and shelled at a river near Kamenica. The witness recalled hearing the sound of a Praga being fired and that there were so many dead bodies that you could step from one to the other one. On 13 July, as the ambush survivors regrouped, the witness recognised many people from his village. Later, amid bursts of gun-fire, they were forced to surrender in the hills above Kamenica. The men were then taken to a meadow which the witness was later told was in Lolici. The witness heard that approximately 2.000 people had been captured. In the meadow the witness recalled seeing a prisoner beaten severely and then killed by a Serb soldier after asking for water. The witness recalled that General Mladic later arrived and addressed the prisoners saying: "Naser has deserted you. He fled to Tuzla. It's not a good idea to fight with a Serb. We have almost evacuated your families. They are accommodated in Tuzla, Kladanj, and another place. Most likely within a day or two you will follow and all of you will be able to find your families. Nobody will beat you, nobody will provoke you. We will provide you -- we will provide food for you. It's very hot where you are. We will find cooler accommodation for you." Following Mladic's speech, the witness and other prisoners were searched and their valuables taken. Within about half an hour of General Mladic's departure, the prisoners were told to line up in a column, four abreast, and march towards Kravica between soldiers positioned at intervals several metres apart on both sides. The witness saw civilians on the road as the prisoners walked towards Kravica. On the way they also passed a UN APC. The witness arrived at the Kravica warehouse at around 16 or 1700 hours. At that time a bus was parked in front of the building which the witness and the other prisoners had to pass behind as they entered. The side of the warehouse where the witness entered was nearly full and the witness sat down amongst the prisoners near a corner against the wall. The warehouse was soon filled and the last prisoner to enter could find no place to sit. A soldier ordered him to do so and then struck and kicked the prisoner. When the prisoner responded that there was no space for him to sit down, the soldier fired a burst into him. At that moment the shooting erupted, coming at the prisoners from all kinds of weapons, which continued into the night. The witness took cover among the dead and lay still in the warehouse, covered in their blood for many hours. Early on 14 July the witness got up to try to get some water but was warned by a neighbour of his to stay down. Later on, the neighbour was killed, having himself momentarily risen in order to urinate. The witness pulled two bodies over himself and remained there the entire day. When it became light, soldiers called for prisoners, saying that they would be taken to hospital. The wounded came out and were killed. The witness recalled that two other prisoners inside the warehouse were also shot down; one after repeatedly calling out someone's name and the other after pleading for water. At a certain point the witness heard commands being given to: "Park the loader, wash the asphalt, cover the dead with hay." The soldiers came into the warehouse and threw hay all over the dead prisoners and the witness who lay among them. The witness later saw this loader parked in front of the warehouse when he escaped. Sometime after midnight, that is, the early morning of 15 July, the witness pulled himself from under the dead bodies. He encountered two other survivors, the first of whom he asked to join in trying to escape. The witness was refused and instead managed to leave the warehouse with the second prisoner undetected. As he fled the witness was spotted by soldiers who called for him to show himself. However, the witness managed to elude capture and made it to a nearby river. From there, together with the second survivor, the witness escaped through a cornfield into the woods. That concludes my summary, Mr. President, and I have a few questions further to put to the witness and some documents -- some exhibits to show him. If I could please have in e-court 65 ter 999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I recognise the warehouse well. I don't recognise it as looking exactly in 1991 or 1992, but I know what it looked like in 1995 when I got there. Now, how it looked like in 1996 and 1997, I don't know that either because I don't know what changes they had made. Because various people photographed it at various times. I don't know what it looked like from the other side. I know what it looked like from the side of the asphalt road by which I came. I passed through the buses -- between the buses and the warehouse. I passed the first entrance door and got into the second entrance door. Two Serb soldiers were standing at the door. I got in and one of my acquaintances motioned me to sit down next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see the entrance door that you went in through in this picture?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Here you see the first door. This could be the second door, but that was not the end of the building. There was more of this warehouse building. This big door is not the one I got inside through. All I know is that I passed one door before I got into the next. This doesn't look exactly like the door I got into, but from which side this picture was taken I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you 65 ter 1003 and then we'll come back to this one in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could blow up more or less the middle of the screen, just make it a little bit larger so he can see it better. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to -- are you able to recognise the door that you came in through in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: This must be the second door. Now, what is this marked with black? From this door on there are more warehouses. This is the first door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to mark this photograph, if you could, if we can have that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Officer will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first door, then this must be the second one. I got in through the second door. But it doesn't appear as it does when you look at it from the asphalt road. It depends from which side this picture was taken. I don't know that. All I know is I passed one door before I got in through the next. The warehouse was packed. I had nowhere to sit down. I had to go into a corner to sit down. There was no room close to the asphalt door. I went to the other end. This could be the first and this could be the second entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you mark the door that you think it might be.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, how is this picture taken? Was it taken from the asphalt road or from the side? Then this must be the second entrance door. I can mark it. There's something like a black blob here. I don't know what it is. All I know is I passed one door and got in through the next. Now, is it really that one? It doesn't look on the picture as I -- as it looked when I went to Srebrenica to put in my application for return. Now, from which side this picture was taken and how -- I mean, everyone can see what these doors looked like. It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just put a circle around the door that you think it might be. That way we can see what you're pointing at, because nobody can see what you're pointing at right now.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: If this is one door, then this is the second door. I don't see any more doors. This must be the door, but it doesn't look as it looked when I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to mark it or do you need some time to look at it? I can show you another exhibit if that will help you remember.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Let's see that other exhibit. Well, we shouldn't be wasting time on this. Everyone can go there and see what it looks like, this warehouse. I know what it looked like when I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you 65 ter 1720. Now, this is a document that you marked some time ago, and I just want to show it to you to see if that helps refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: From the side of the asphalt road, the building runs parallel to it, whereas here we have some corners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just blow it up on the right side where you can see the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you have the first entrance door. This is the first entrance door and this is the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which is the second? Can you describe what you see?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: This one here. I can see the first and the second doors. There they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the second door to the left or to the right in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Both doors face the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness. Is the first door to the right of the picture or to the left of the picture?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: As we reached the building from Lolici, we were on the left-hand side to the road, because to the right flows the river. If we were to head towards Lolici, then it would be to the right of the asphalt road and to the left of the river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps it will help everybody if you can make --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I reached the building, the warehouse was to my right, so I passed by the first door and then got in through the second door, and I was between the warehouse and the parking-lot where the buses stood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, I understand very well. But could you please for our help put a cross at the first door you were pointing at, just a cross at the first door. Which was it? The door you passed by and headed to the second door, which was the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then perhaps you can put a circle above the second door where you entered the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is now understandable for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like actually to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- tender this document, and then I would like to go back to the other ones and tender those as well because I think it's apparent from those other photos what he's marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked photo will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the first document I showed the witness was 65 ter 999, and I would like to tender that document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a request to make so that we do not torment the witness. We can do it this way this once. However, in the future, I think we should refrain from showing witnesses photographs that had already been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's helpful to put a photo with markings to a witness, or a map. In this case I think it was an appropriate way to find out which door was the substance of the evidence. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I had -- was about to refer to or had referred to 65 ter 1003. That was the second photograph I think I showed the witness, and I would like to tender that witness [sic] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is already an exhibit, P262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was part of the four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is I'd like to have it back on the screen. I'd like to show the witness and ask him some questions about that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are waiting for P262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are some technical problems, as I'm told, but it comes up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could just focus a little bit on the right side of the photograph and blow that -- the left side, I'm sorry, of the photograph and blow that up a little bit. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, what I wanted to do was draw your attention to the bottom of this photograph. Do you see what appears to be a fence at the bottom of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it here. At the time I did not see a fence, however. Perhaps fences and walls were added afterwards, but when I got there I didn't see a fence. I know what the warehouse looked like when I got there. I don't know what it looked like later. I know what my house looked like before I left and what it looked like when I got back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify whether or not there was a fence when you arrived there in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, in a previous statement you mentioned that inside the warehouse there was a small room. Do you remember speaking about that back in 1996?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I remember. On the night of Thursday, they were beating us inside. I thought I heard water running. I stood up and I had this vision of some sort of a room, but a neighbour of mine stopped me from going away. He told me, "Sit down, there is no water here." I don't know what happened to me. Was I so frightened or deranged that I thought I heard water running, though I never saw any water in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do -- well, there's two things. In your answer it's translated that you said: "On the night of Thursday, they were beating us ..." I just want to make sure that's an accurate translation of what you said. Were you being beaten on the night of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: They started beating us on Thursday between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon and continued until the night fell. Shots were heard. The wounded who could help others did. We could hear them outside the warehouse laughing throughout the night. In the morning, as it dawned, I don't know what time of day it was, they called to us and said, "If there's anyone alive, come out." Some of them -- some of them came out, I don't know how many. I didn't look up to see. I heard a truck engine start. I don't know where it went. Silence fell in the warehouse then. At some point during the day, a voice could be heard shouting, "Salko." Some 15 to 20 times this individual was calling out to Salko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to know when you say "beating," you mean shooting or you mean beating without -- without weapons?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Shooting. They were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: From automatic weapons, machine-guns, with hand-grenades, rifle-launch grenades. When this person called out to Salko, we could hear his Turkish mother being sworn at and a shot fired. Then silence fell again. Then a voice could be heard shouting, "Adila, water, Adila, water." Again oaths could be heard swearing his Turkish mother and shots followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Those who were only wounded and got out to get on the truck, they were killed in front of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- I want to focus you, if I could, just for a moment on this small room. And I'd like to show you a photograph. It's 65 ter 1450 and it's page 105. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: You can show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's -- the exhibit number, I'm sorry, is P94, and it will be page 105 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to show you this photograph for a moment.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't recall this photograph at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I want to ask you about - if we can just zoom out a little bit, that's it - is if you can see on the left side of the photograph there's an apparent entry. And in the photograph you can see what appears to be the outline of a wall. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Is it outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is the inside of the warehouse and what you see there on the left side is a doorway leading outside.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: This wall -- I don't know the photograph at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is: The outline of this wall in relation to the door, is that -- does that approximate the position of the small room that you saw while you were in the warehouse relative to the door?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't remember the photograph at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was the room that you saw in the warehouse near the door?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the photograph anymore. I just want to know: Was the room that you saw inside the warehouse near the doorway?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I mentioned this room where I thought I heard water running, but I never reached the water or this reception room I thought I saw because the person next to me pulled me down and said that I should stay on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it would be perhaps helpful to remove this photo from the screen because there is some confusion, and the witness clearly indicated that he doesn't remember and recognise this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's better not to have it on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and then you may continue with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember having mentioned this small room to an OTP investigator in 1996?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I remember mentioning this room and saying that I thought I heard water running in that room when I was in the warehouse. I was close by this room and I got up to reach it but was pulled back by the person who was lying next to me who said, "There's no water around here." So I do remember clearly thinking that I heard water. Was I so thirsty that I conjured it up? I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the investigator that the room was on the left side of the entrance to the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I had this idea that it was to the left, to my left, but I never reached it. It was night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: And in the course of the day I didn't move a finger. I stayed put where I was. I don't know what happened. I know that throughout the night when they were shooting at us they were outside the warehouse, and then in the morning, they called out to the wounded to come out, that they would board a bus. And then they shot them all, including the person who called to Salko and the other one who was asking for water. And then for the following 24 hours, not a soul could be heard in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much, Witness. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Mr. President. Thanks again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Sir, now the accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to put questions to you. And now, Mr. Tolimir, start your cross-examination. But again, sir, if you need a break, just tell us. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to all those present in the courtroom. Peace unto all of them and unto this house and may this trial reflect God's will. Greetings to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us clarify several points rather than go through the entire statement. In the second sentence of the summary, Prosecutor Vanderpuye said that the witness was captured and was with 1.200 Muslims who were killed in Kravica. Since I don't want to take you through the entire statement and -- and you gave your statement in 2000. So can you tell me what is the difference between what Mr. Vanderpuye read out and what you said in your statement. Is there a difference? I just want to know because I don't want your statement to have its value detracted simply because one piece of information does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't understand at all what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you how many people were shot with you in this warehouse that you didn't recognise here?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't count them. I never tried to count them. I know that we were seated in Lolici and that those who were in front of me were saying that there were around 2.000 people there. All of them were forced to the warehouse and none came out alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I've understood what you've said. In other words, based on the assessment of those you spoke to, you drew your conclusion as to how many there were?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell you whether there were a thousand more or less. I heard their estimate that there were around 2.000 people there. I don't want to go into whether this was correct or not. I only know that all of those who were with me in the column, none survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm happy with your answer. I merely wanted to clarify this at the outset.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D85. This is the statement given by the witness to the Ministry of the Interior, the State Security Service of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I gave you a moment now to look at the statement that you gave. When did you find out that you were supposed to go to the village of Jaglici? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you when did you find out, what was the date, and if you can also tell me who it was you found it out from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. It should not be broadcast out of the courtroom. So the accused asked you the following question: When did you find out, what was the date, and if you can also tell him who was you found it out from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean that we were supposed to leave Srebrenica and our home? It was on the 11th of July that I learned this. I was on my estate gathering hay, and my daughter came to see me and said, "What are you doing? People are leaving. Srebrenica has fallen." I went home. I let the cattle out of the barn, and I met my brother-in-law, whose house had been burnt in 1991, early on, and had spent all this time in exile at my home. He asked me, "Where are you going?" And I said, "I want to release the cattle." He said that he had already done so. So I took a rucksack, collected some clothes and food, as much as could fit the rucksack. And on the 11th of July I left my home. It was in the early evening hours. It may have been 7.00 or 8.00. They told us women, children, and the elderly were supposed to go to the UN camp in Potocari, whereas those who were able-bodied were supposed to toward Tuzla and the assembly point would be in Jaglici. I said good-bye to my wife and the two daughters above Ravne Njive. They set out towards Potocari and I set out towards Jaglici. I spent the night there. In the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, may I interrupt you. Excuse me. The answer -- the question of the accused was answered, I think, so that Mr. Tolimir has perhaps another question for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we call up 1D87 in e-court, page 2. Let's look at page 1 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the statement given to the ICTY. It's your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's turn to page 2, line 8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will skip the first and second paragraphs and go to the eighth line. "A day or two before the fall of Srebrenica, I heard a rumour that the enclave was about to fall. Our commander," and I will not read his name, "informed us that we would have to break the corridor to proceed towards Tuzla. The women, children, elderly, and the sick or injured had to go to Potocari. "My daughters and my wife went to Potocari the 11th of July." Did I correctly quote your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not true that I learnt two days earlier. I learned on the 11th of July that Srebrenica had fallen. I was at my family farm. I learned that the women, children, and the elderly should go to Potocari and we should go to Tuzla. I would have gone to Potocari too, but my rucksack and my food-supply had already been shipped out on horseback of a friend, so I had to follow. I would have liked to go to Potocari too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, but you say you found out on the 11th, but you also say: "Our commander ... informed us that we would have to break the corridor to proceed towards Tuzla." Who is the commander, because his name is redacted, who told you you needed to open up a corridor?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: When we got to Jaglici, I don't know how many people had gathered there already. It was an enumerable mass and they said, "Let's go to Tuzla to break through, and then who passes, passes, and those who don't, tough luck." There were six -- Srebrenica was a protected area, but it had better not had been because we would have fought and we would have fought with tooth and nail to defend ourselves. But instead, we had relaxed because we had been living in a protected area. Well, didn't they go Srebrenica, Zepa, Zvornik, and other areas to be evacuated? How many poor people remained fatherless? How many children don't know what they fathers looked like?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, for the record, tell us, who told you to break-through towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursunovic told us to go into a break-through, to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Commander, our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mean of some kind of brigade of yours?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, of course. It certainly wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we go back to 1D --

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Can we have a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness wants a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Then in that case we should have a break now and I think that should be the first break, a little bit earlier than usual, and we resume quarter to 4.00. The Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I hope very much that you are now in a better condition. I would like to remind you to tell us immediately if there is another break needed for you. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his questioning for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May the witness be shown 1D87 in e-court, page 2, lines 21 through 25. And when the witness has read it I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Court Officer told the relevant persons not to broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, in the third paragraph from the top you say: "In Jaglici," that's line 21, "we arrived in Jaglici around 2200 hours."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was when we arrived. It was night, but I can't say whether it was 8.00 p.m. or 10.00 p.m. I know when we set out from -- to Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading your statement. These are your words. You gave that statement to the investigator. You said: "We arrived at Jaglici around 2200 hours."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't remember. I know we arrived after nightfall, but I can't tell you at what time. I know we set out to Jaglici on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will just quote a passage and then I'll ask you a question, and then you can answer whatever you like. Now, please wait for me to give you the quotation. In line 21, I quote: "We arrived at Jaglici at night around 2200 hours. People were forming a column and started to move towards the woods. "The first groups were supposed to clean the mines so we had to wait. The soldiers were mixed with the civilians but the civilians were concentrated in the middle of the column." And my question is: Did you say this to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I did give the statement, but I didn't have a watch then and I don't know what time we arrived at Jaglici. I know what time we set out from Jaglici because I knew a forester whom I knew. I ask him, "What time is it?" He said, "It's 20 to 1.00."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not important. Just tell me, did you say this to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I did say this, but I didn't say the time when we arrived at Jaglici. I said to them at what time we set out from Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us something about the forming of this column you mentioned in this sentence I just quoted. We started moving towards the woods. The first groups were supposed to clean mines. Soldiers were mixed with civilians. The civilians were in the middle. Can you tell us more about how this column was formed. I said can you tell us how this column was formed?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I know I set out from Jaglici in a column of people. It was not all of 6 metres wide. We went three or four abreast up to a place called Buljim. I didn't know that place. We went downhill to a macadam road. On that road the column was already moving and there was a valley ahead with people standing there. I don't know what they were waiting for. When we got down to the road there was a man, perhaps he was the last man from Jaglici with that group, and he was getting down to the macadam road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question and then you can go on? Please. Tell me, since you were a soldier --

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I was not a soldier. I was in civilian clothes. I had my hunting rifle up to Jaglici, and at Jaglici my brother-in-law took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you were of the right age to be a military conscript because it says here you were working in a depot.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: What depot?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then I'll have to quote all of these statements where you said you worked in the rear, in the logistics.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I was a member, but I was in the civilian protection. And when I moved to Tuzla, I was at Stupari in the logistics. I chopped wood, I brought food and water until 1996. In 1996, I was demobed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show 1D87, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's the sentence below the first paragraph. It's a simple sentence. You said: "I joined the army on the 17th of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: In 1996. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May I note for the record that from 1992 until 1996 you were a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you formed that column, how come civilians and -- came and then soldiers came? Did somebody give you orders and commands?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: We were moving like cattle. Nobody was paying attention to anyone up to that place, Buljim. And then we ran into an ambush, and then people dispersed. Nobody took -- paid any attention to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 1D85, line 8, page 1 -- sorry, page 2. In fact, that's the first page of the statement. Line 8 in 1D85.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see the first paragraph on 11 July, then the second paragraph starts with on 12 July, and then further down it says around --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused give us an exact reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "Until about 1200 hours the column was lining up and forming ..."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, we would line up and then disperse and then line up again. What exactly was going on, I don't know. They would line us up, but we are not moving anywhere. We dispersed again and then finally we set out towards Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before you moved to Buljim, tell us how long this lining up took because you said you arrived around 2200 hours. Did it last until midnight?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I did not say at what time we arrived at Jaglici. I didn't have a watch. I didn't even know -- I mean, I wouldn't even have known when we set out from Jaglici if I hadn't asked that forester for the time. And he said 20 to 1.00, 20 to 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And when did you arrive at Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: It was after nightfall. I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it true what you said in the statement, that you arrived at 2200 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: When did I say it was 10.00 p.m., when? I know when -- I know that we arrived at Jaglici after nightfall, but I never said to anyone at what time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show 1D87, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I remind you not to overlap and wait for the end of the translation. You can always see it on the screen. It's very difficult for the recorder and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked for 1D87, page 2, in the Serbian language to be shown, line 21. We just had it on the screen a moment ago. And it's the same page number in English. I will quote the sentence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is your statement. It says "Witness Statement" at the top. And in line 21: "We arrived at Jaglici at night around 2200 hours. People were forming a column." I'm not making this up. I'm just reading your statement and that statement was given to the ICTY, this Tribunal here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have quoted this portion already earlier, and the witness gave you an answer. It's not necessary to repeat it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I insisted, but the witness said that he never said it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say at what time we arrived at night at Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is your statement.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: You can write what you like. I know what I said. I know what time I set out from Jaglici, but at what time I came, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your statement. I didn't make anything up.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I didn't make anything up either, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, how long did it take to form this column, because you don't remember when you arrived and you remember when you set out at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: We arrived at 20 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Stop thanking me. You're asking me questions here. Whatever I said, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry that I keep saying "thank you," but I always have to say "thank you" at the end of a question.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: You don't need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Never mind. Tell me how long did this column take to form, because you know you set out at 20 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I wasn't at the head of the column or at the end of the column, at the tail, I was somewhere in the middle. In that column, we went to Buljim, and there was a delay when we arrived up to that point because there was a crowd of people there. I don't know what they were waiting for. We were standing on the macadam road outside Buljim, and then a man came out and said, "What are we waiting for?" And somebody answered, "We lost track of the column." The other man said, cursing everyone's mother and children, saying, "Now I'll show you the track of the column." I don't know who that man was. I asked my fellow standing next to me, "Who is this?" And the man answered, "Golic." And that's when I saw this Golic for the first and last time. On the left side of the hill somebody started cursing, "What are we waiting for?" And then shooting started. People immediately dispersed. Nobody's looking at anyone else, nobody's looking for mines. I ran down with my fellow down to a river. There were people lying dead or wounded. Nobody was looking at them, paying the least attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question relating to what you just said. You just mentioned Golic. Do you mean Ejub Golic, commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I never heard of any other Golic and I didn't know that man until then, until that other person told me, "This is Ejub Golic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Golic address you? Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: No, he just addressed the person who told him that they had lost track of the column, and that's all before the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are still waiting for the translation of the answer. Please pause before you put the next question. You are always overlapping. It is not appropriate behaviour. Please pause. Now continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm trying to make a pause to mark the end of my question, but the witness doesn't want me to say thank you, he doesn't want to wait either, so please make the same request to him and everything will be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is not a question of the words "thank you," but look at the screen. You see on the transcript when the recording stopped. And then put the next question and not earlier. This is very simple. It is very simple. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I can't follow the transcript because all the three screens in front of me are adjusted to the documents. Not one of them is adjusted to show the transcript. I tried to handle it myself. It's either the transcript or the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you could press the button "LiveNote," you will have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm currently dealing with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have now the transcript in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Mr. President. I can have either the transcript or the documents. I can't have both. The Legal Officer has just tried to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I understand your difficulties, Mr. Tolimir, but there is a way to solve this problem. If you just pause a little bit more, you will perhaps realise that we are still receiving the translation and then pause a little bit and not immediately put the next question. Then I think everything will be fine. Please carry on with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can you tell me, please, how much time do I have left, since time has so far been spent in a manner that wasn't rational?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think -- I didn't count it. You indicated two and a half or three hours for the whole cross-examination. I think that will be sufficient for you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago you mentioned Zulfo Tursunovic and said that he was your commander. Was he Naser Oric's deputy or not, can you tell the Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't. I suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was Ramiz Becirovic, can you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I can't tell you what role Ramiz Becirovic had. At any rate, he was in Srebrenica. I don't know who he was. Was he in the staff or in the command? I don't know. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who lined up the column? Was it Zulfo Tursunovic? Was it Ramiz or another person?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I didn't see either Ramiz or Zulfo there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, do you know at all where the HQ of the BH army in Srebrenica was before you left it?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Where the headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarters of the 21st Division in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, nowhere. Wherever somebody happened to be, that's where it was. There were six municipalities there and nobody knew what was going on. It was a protected enclave and the people let their guard down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the command of the 28th Division was and were you ever in the command?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I was never there. I didn't know exactly where the seat of the division was or how it was called. I was a farmer. I tilled the land, and when it fell upon me to take my duty I would do so. Otherwise, I would rest. I didn't have time to go to Srebrenica to see what was going on, and I wasn't that interested either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the 11th of July, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it ever happen to you that you have to go to -- that you had to go to the front line or take up any other duty within the BH army since you were a member of the army up until 1996?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Sometimes at night I would have to stand guard, but during the day, I had to stay on my farm because there weren't enough people to do the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt. I think -- if we could just go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. I will do my best and I don't think that the Defence did anything to reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Page 7080, line -- lines 8 and 9 from the witness's testimony in Popovic et al., the witness said the following, I quote: "I was occupied with hay-making on that day and my daughter came to me and said that our neighbour had been killed and that an order had been issued for us to leave, since Srebrenica had fallen." At page 7138, lines 12 through 19 of the transcript in the Popovic case, in answer to a question put by one of the Defence counsel, and I'll quote the question: "Is it fair to say that on the 11th of July, 1995, you received information via courier that Srebrenica had fallen and that women, children, and the elderly should go to Potocari and the others should take to the woods?" And you said, I'm quoting your answer: "Yes, I think that I said that." Question from the Defence counsel: "You received this information from your commander, Zulfo Tursunovic, who told you that you should open a corridor to Tuzla?" Your answer to that was: "Yes." Did I accurately quote the exchange between you and one of the Defence counsel in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you understand the question of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And he wanted to know if he quoted your testimony in the Popovic case correctly. Can you answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tolimir wanted to know from you if he quoted your evidence, your testimony in the Popovic case correctly. Could you answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I said everything clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when and where did the courier let you know that you should leave your village and set out to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I think that I said that I was on my farm hay-making when my daughter came and said that people were leaving. I think that I've repeated this countless times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case you said that you received the information from your commander, Zulfo Tursunovic, and that he told you --

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: He sent a courier. I said that I was on my farm and my daughter came and informed me that we should leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand what you're saying. Is the following correct. Your daughter conveyed to you the order sent by Tursu through a courier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this understanding of Mr. Tolimir correct? Are you able to answer, sir, or is it very difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tolimir wanted to know if he understood you correctly that your daughter conveyed the order of Mr. Tursunovic to form a column was conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through a courier. Not that a column should be formed from the village, but that we should set out towards Potocari and toward Jaglici. Please don't put one and the same question to me five times. I said quite clearly that we set out, including women, children, and the elderly, all the way through to Ravne Njive. From Ravne Njive, women, children, and the elderly set out to Potocari, and we set out to the woods. I think that that's the long and the short of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That helps Mr. Tolimir, I think. You should move to another topic, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've mentioned Ravne Njive as the place where women and children went their way to Potocari, including your daughter. Can you tell us who did the separating and who told you to do so?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: We received the order as soon as we set out from the village that the elderly, women, and children should go to Potocari and that the rest should go to Jaglici, where we would assemble. I think that I've explained it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But this was the first time you mentioned Ravne Njive?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: No, I don't know how many times I've mentioned it as the place where we separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the 28th Mountain Battalion in Srebrenica commanded by Ejub Golic and where it was in the column?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I said where I saw Ejub Golic for the first and last time, and I said it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case at page 7133 of the transcript, lines 3 to 4, you said, and I quote: "As far as I was able to see, his group was the last to leave Jaglici, I believe." You were referring to Ejub Golic. Did Captain Ejub Golic with the 28th Mountain Battalion form part of the column? Was he at the front or at the rear end of the column?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that because I didn't know Ejub and I said so quite clearly. When he came to Buljim with a group of people, I don't think anybody else was left behind at Jaglici, and then I explained what happened afterwards. And that's the last time I'm going to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic case at 7109 page of the transcript, lines 19 through 25, and page 7110, lines 1 to 2, you said, and I quote: "It was a long column. Ejub was the next person to arrive and I think that he was the next to set out from Jaglici. As for Buljim, I don't know if they stopped there. I continued roaming [as interpreted] that day. When Ejub arrived he said, 'What are you waiting for?' We told him that we lost track of the column. And he said, 'What are you waiting for here?' And then he cursed our mothers. All at once shooting started from the left and the right. People dispersed without paying attention to one another, without paying attention to either the wounded or the dead. Everybody tried to save their necks." And I was quoting your words from the Popovic case. This is my question: Why did Ejub Golic curse? Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I suppose because we lost track of the column. We weren't proceeding on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: There is -- there was no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now look at transcript page 7114, lines 10 through 12. Your testimony is recorded there which needs clarifying because it may have been misinterpreted. You'll tell us that and I'll quote what you said. "As far as I know, we were the only ones in civilian uniform who had formed the column."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one. There was several of us in civilian uniform rather than military uniform. There were more of us in civilian rather than military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said that there were more of you in civilian clothes rather than uniforms. Does this mean that soldiers were also dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, those who had them put them on; those who didn't, didn't put them on. That's the short of it. Not everyone had them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the issue of ambushes, in your statements you mentioned two ambushes. At transcript page 7133, lines 9 through 11, in the Popovic case, you said that: "The first ambush took place close to the place called Buljim, where I saw Golic. That was where the people dispersed. The second ambush took place when we reached the river." This is my question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused switch his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall where the first ambush took place and do you recall what the landscape was like there?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I told you that it was below Buljim, just outside Buljim. There was a macadam road at the foot of the hill there, and that's where the first ambush took place. The second ambush took place in the evening hours above Kamenica. We were going downstream along the river. There were a group of five or six persons. We stopped there as shooting started from one of the hills. Fire was opened from a Praga. We set out toward the place where we heard the shooting from and shouts. We were maybe some 300 metres away from the place where shooting could be heard as well as shouts. We could not pass through there, so we returned. We heard bullets whizzing past our heads. I came across a tree and hid behind it. I could be hit only from the air and not from the side because I was sheltered behind the tree. I thought that the others were around me as well. I stood up and there were occasional bursts of fire to be heard, and I realised that none of those who were there with me previously were there any longer. I lost my cap. I didn't know how it happened. I started walking toward the place where the shooting could be heard. I had passed some 100 to 200 metres before I shouted, "Don't shoot. I'm one of yours." I don't know who was on the other side, but they were waiting for me to come. I -- as I came closer, I saw that there was a young man. He said, "Old man, I see that you have something in your rucksack. I'm hungry." I told him that I had some bread and meat. He had something to eat and then we left the place. As we were walking, we realised we were treading on dead bodies, and I recognised one of those to be my neighbour. And I asked the young man who was with me to give me a match or a lighter so that I could make some light to see if this was indeed my neighbour, but the young man left. I no longer saw him. Then I heard shouts from a group down near the brook, shouting, "Help." When it dawned, we were collecting wounded down there. We realised that we were close to Kamenica, that's what they said. And I saw that they were lining up there but I went past them to their right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you gave a lengthy answer to the question of the accused that was very helpful, but I think Mr. Tolimir has the right to put another question to you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't want to interrupt you, but can you tell us how many people got killed in the first ambush and how many in the second, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I didn't count them and I wouldn't be able to find an individual who would be able to count the dead. It was night-time when the first ambush took place. As for the second, there were dead and wounded, but I can't tell you how many. Well, I could tell you there were 50 or a hundred. I could tell you anything since I didn't count them, and I can't tell you what I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D86, page 3 in Serbian and English, line 22 from the top, line 22 and the following lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a statement given to the state commission of the BH on the 22nd of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. It will come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me quote your words. "The second ambush took place above Buljim."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Above Buljim, out of the question. Above Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're right. "The second ambush took place above Bratunacka Kamenica. Shooting started from all sides and I found shelter in a ditch, waiting for nightfall. I set out along ferns and came across a young man called Fuad. I gave him some food and proceeded to join our own people. It seemed to me that there were 500 dead bodies" --

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that there were 500 dead bodies. I only said that it seemed that -- like you were treading on dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible that the typist added himself the number of 500?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, he could have put 1.000 and 5.000 there. I know that I didn't say a number because I did not count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can document 1D086 be shown at page 3, or rather, this page and this witness statement may be added in the transcript that this isn't something that the witness said, that it was entered into the statement against his will. Can this document be admitted into evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, everything what the witness says is on the transcript. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D45, under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If I can quote what you just said, you said that there were a great many dead but you did not count them.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I said that there were many dead bodies and that as I walked I was treading on bodies; and I didn't count them, I was not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have your handwritten statement in e-court, that's page 9 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be shown?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the number. 1D86, page 3, sixth line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I'm quoting what you wrote in your hand. "It seems to me that there were 500 dead bodies."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I said that I didn't count them and that I didn't give a number, but you can write whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't write it. This is your handwriting. Look at it. You have it in front of you on the screen. It's line 6. "It seems to me that there were 500 dead bodies."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't recall saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But is this your handwriting, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Just like you say the second ambush was outside Buljim and it was outside Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you help us, please. On the right side of the screen, there you can see a document in handwriting. Was that done by you or by somebody else? Is that your handwriting? I think you should look on the right screen. Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender this document into evidence for us to see that this witness denied it was his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, he didn't deny that this is his statement. He just said it is not his handwriting. And we have already received it as D45, under seal. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us who wrote this statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The one on the right-hand side of the monitor, the manuscript, who wrote it if it's not you?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I did not write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement and somebody writing your words down?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I gave a statement that I saw dead bodies, but I didn't give a figure. How could I have possibly counted the dead in pitch dark?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand that, but you can answer my question with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I said I did not count the bodies and I did not give a figure for the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm just asking who wrote this statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote it. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know we've gone around on this one for quite some time now, but if we go to page 7 there's a clear indication of who the statement was taken down by. It's actually translated in English as well. If the exhibit is already in evidence, I suppose it would be all right to read it and I'll tell you what it says. It says: "Statement taken by Erna Lucic," and then there's a clerk signature and then there's a statement given by the witness. And if you look at the actual exhibit written in the B/C/S, it's very clear. You can identify different handwriting on the document itself. You can see the witness's name written down on the document. You can see the person who took the statement's name written down on the document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be even easier to have page 7 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is the first page and not page 7. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. That's page 1. Page 7 is ERN ending 2281. That's 6 -- page 6, I think, in e-court. If we just go down to where the stamp is -- we're not broadcasting this, right? Right. If we go down to the stamp and blow it up, you can see the witness's name very clearly. And we can go to the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which page of the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ah, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have it as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can very clearly see the people who are involved in the making and the taking of the statement, which frankly corresponds to what the witness has testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have again on the screen that page with -- to which Mr. Tolimir was referring about the 500 dead bodies, in Serbian and in English. I don't know which page it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The document is 1D086.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the page because Mr. Tolimir was speaking over the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, it's page 9 in e-court, if you mean the document which is a manuscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On top of this page we have now on the screen in English and in B/C/S the handwritten version. Do you have any further questions related to this document, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no questions, but I would like the witness to confirm that he did not give the number 500, that it's the commission who took the statement that put in the number, which was a state commission. They wrote the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who wrote it. I didn't write that figure. That's the most important thing. Because I was not able to count. Let's get that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have the answer very clear on the record. Mr. Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would just like to check something regarding the authenticity of this handwritten document. Could I see the last page, please. Madam Usher, could I see the last page with the signature on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you read the last paragraph in your language, please. Are you able to do that? I can then listen to the interpretation into French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is written here I cannot make out at all. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a shame. Never mind. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But could you tell us if the signature on the right side on the bottom, if you recognise this signature. Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it. I can read the text, but I didn't write it, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You see a name there, a signature. Have you made this signature or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember writing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this signature similar to your normal signature as you use it if you sign a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually write block letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Even if you sign a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually sign in block letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can leave this topic here and, Mr. Tolimir, you shall continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we show 1D85 to the witness in e-court to see the signature of this witness, where he uses block letters not italics, and that shows that this one is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, this is my signature in block letters. Most of the time I write in block letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: That I wrote something, I didn't write anything. I can recognise this signature. Now, what's written on top, I don't care. I know what I've seen, I know what I've survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Are you tendering this document, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D46, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show document 1D085, page 3 in both Serbian and English, the last paragraph but one. It's a statement given by this witness to the State Security Service of the Ministry of the Interior in Tuzla on the 27 October 2010 [as interpreted]. There it is on the screen but we need the next page in English, not the one on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're looking at the last paragraph but one. I'll quote the last five lines, but I will not read out the place names. Although you can see the place names on the screen, I will avoid identifying you. I quote: "In Jelah I found Sacir and Kasim whose last name I don't know. Both of them from the village of ... Bratunac municipality and we went off together towards ... and after that to ... on 29 July 1995 ... fell and I returned to ... together with 14 other people where we stayed for 42 days. And after that. Ten of us went towards Kladanj and we arrived there on 18 September 1995."

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I did not mention Sacir and Kasim. I said Kasim and Sacir I found in Jelah. Not Secan but Sacir and Kasim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. So it's Sacir and Kasim from Bratunac municipality. I want your answer to this question, though: How many of you in total set out to that place in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: From Pobudje, only I, Sacir, and Kasim from Jelah. We spent the night in Jelah. Somewhere above the village, on the hill above Jelah, shooting started. I didn't know this place Pobudje. Ramiz took us there, and there I parted ways with Sacir and Kasim. Sacir wanted to stay on the asphalt roads to Cerska and Baljkovica, and when we set out he asks me, "Do you know the road?" I said, "I don't know, I would need to see where Rogac was to find my way." However, we set out and we ran into a young man who was running from the other direction. We asked, "Is there anyone left there?" He answered, "No one. Everyone took to the woods. They lived on what they could find in the woods, roasting snails and mushrooms." We asked him, "Are you from Jagodnja? Do you know that forester Hasim?" He says, "No." How many children does he have? Three. What's his wife's name? We told him the wife's name. And he says, "I'll join you and go with you." We went on. We ran into some dead bodies on the road or along the road, eight or nine bodies.
