Then we went up the hill. "Do you know where Rahunici is?" And he says, "Rahunici is up there, where the mosque used to be." So we went downhill towards Rahunici. There was a wire fence with a berry field inside and we went on to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: May I just stop you here. Where did you see those nine bodies?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: In Pobudje, overlooking Jelah. I don't know what that hill overlooking Jelah was. They were lying down. One of them had his legs stuck on to sticks around the tree. Somebody said there were nine bodies, but I saw eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this text that I just quoted, how did you find yourself with 14 other persons? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: There were no 14 people. There were three of us, and when we walked along the fence around the berry field, we ran into one more person. He said, "Where are you going?" He said we were going along Sutjeska towards Zepa. He says, "There were many ambushes there. You can't get through." I said, "I'm going to a place I know." He says, "You're crazy." And I say, "If I'm crazy, you don't have to join me." This young man went away and I never saw him again. We spent the night at Rahunici and set out again in the morning. Neither of us knew the road. We emerged at a road near the hill used for transporting wood. I saw a cemetery and some bunkers, and on one aim there was a name, Mehir or Menir. We went on top of the hill. I saw a linden tree. I said Rogac must be there, and the other man said, "If you're sure, let's go." We came to a valley. There were eight heads of cattle there. We did not dare go through the valley, fearing that we might run into a shepherd or something. And just after the valley I told them, "Sit down here, I'll climb atop a hill to see where we were." I realised that we were close to a place called Sebiocina and I went down to join my fellows and said, "I know where we are now." But we waited first for the dark and headed out towards Rogac. We found the nearest road just near the church via Vojvodici village, through a wood, and we passed the Ljubin mill and we got to that linden tree. I said, "Janko Brezanici's house is here. It's dangerous, he has dangerous dogs." We took a side road towards Kostraca --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us, how many are you at this point?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Three of us. And there we heard a voice or perhaps it was the sound of an animal, like a sheep or something. I said, "There must be a pen or a barn here." I said, "Let's go around," and we found ourselves in a meadow, the grass has not -- had not been mown yet. Perhaps ten minutes later another two persons appeared at the spot where we were standing. I kept my silence, but Sacir said, "Do you see anything?" I said, "I do." And he asks, "What are we going to do?" I said, "Maybe there are people." He said, "How would they be here?" I said, "The same way we were." And we moved towards them, but they were still not seeing us. The last among us slipped and fell onto the ground. As they were moving towards us, we realised they had rucksacks on their backs. When they came close, we saw one of them had an automatic rifle trained at us. They asked, "Who are you and where are you from?" Sacir said, "I'm from Bratunac municipality." And when -- and the other person said then, "If you are a Muslim, then you must know a Muslim prayer, tell it to me." And the other one started telling. And then I recognised the voice and I said, "Is it you Velja?" And he said, "Were you there when the shooting started? Did you hear the shooting?" I said, "We did." They said, "They were shooting at us." Then we found ourselves in a meadow. They had come probably to move the herd or something. They -- Ramiz was hurt. Apparently he was shot in the back, so from that point on we were four.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who is Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Ramiz Becirovic, a younger man. It's not the Ramiz Becirovic you seem to be asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you come to the point when you were 14?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: The four of us got to Zepa, and in Zepa we arrived on the 26th. On the 29th, Zepa fell. I spent eight days in Zepa. And a group formed there, including me, to go to Tuzla. We got to Zalisina. Three of our men stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These men who went with you, were they from Zepa or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: There were some from Bratunac municipality, from Srebrenica municipality, and Vlasenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said ten of you arrived to the territory controlled by the BH army. What happened to the last four?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Three of us, three of that group with which we set out, they remained in Zalisina. Two of us got killed in Stedric, they stepped on mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These who stayed behind, did they stay alone?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, alone, but they crossed over. We did not have enough food. We didn't have any food, so we first had to find food and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mean those two saved themselves?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: They crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Those three who got killed, how did they get killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: They stepped on mines in Stedric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know what their names are?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Abid from Piric, I don't know his last name; and from Mostahovina village it's Samir or Amir, I couldn't tell you exactly. Salim, Salim, those two stepped on the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were these villages around Zepa or Srebrenica or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Mostahovina and the other one was from Piric village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So 12 of you got out. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: After those two got killed in Stedric. I think eight of us moved on from there and then we were in Srebrenica. One group from Udric returned and we were together with them from then on. We hid until the 9th of September. On the 9th of September towards -- we went towards Tuzla and on the 18th I came to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How large was that group?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Quite a few came from Udric, but four or five of them only joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And how many in total returned from Udric?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know how many joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are they all from that column that started out from Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Of course. They were not able to get through, so they came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how many people were wandering about starving?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the number. There were groups and groups in these woods that I never even ran across, people I didn't know. They were wandering around the forests. Some of them set out earlier, some after me. All I know, I was in Kladanj on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there more of them who got through to the other side?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Yes, some set out later than me, like Ramiz Muskic who left with me from the same warehouse and then eventually he stepped on a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In Baljkovica; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We come back to that. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could just go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were in Zepa. Were you in Zepa proper, and did you mingle with the army or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: We were at Igrisnik and Vukovin Stan [phoen] because Zepa had fallen by then. We were in the woods and hills, not in villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted you to draw a distinction between Zepa and the villages you were at.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, all this was under the control of Zepa. These are the villages of Luka, Krusev Do, and we were up in the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you try to get in touch with the forces pulling out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: No. When Zepa fell, the villages of Luka and Krusev Do, there were people from Bratunac municipality and Srebrenica municipality that started going back. There was a large group of I don't know how many people heading for the Drina River, for Serbia. A friend of mine joined them. He wanted me to come along, and I said that I would not venture there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you referring to the group from Srebrenica or the group from Zepa that left for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, there were people from Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Zepa who were part of the group that went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you say that those who went to Serbia, toward the Drina River, managed to survive?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I know of one man who had set out for Serbia and who did not arrive there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know his name and why didn't he get there?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: His name was Nazif Krlic [phoen] from Krusevo, that's the municipality of Srebrenica, but it was part of the Zepa enclave during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know what became of him?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: I don't know. Was he killed? Did he die? At any rate, he never showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What were the stories about people who went for Serbia, did they survive or were they killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I know of this one individual who joined this group, but I didn't know the rest, and I knew of him and I knew that he was the one who didn't arrive there. For the rest, I know that they did reach Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My advisor told me that the name of the person you were referring to was not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I didn't even say this bit about him not arriving there. When the people who had reached Serbia were transferred to the United States, to Australia, and abroad, I learned that Nazif Krlic was the one who did not get there, since he was the one I knew from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many people from Srebrenica saved themselves by leaving Zepa for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PW-005
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the figure. I didn't know how many set out to begin with. I only know who got there of those who I'm acquainted with. I know that Nazif Krlic, one of the Srebrenica men I knew, did not get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to thank the witness and tell him that I have completed my examination of him. I wish him a safe journey home, and safe life where he resides. Thank you and thank all those who helped me to complete the examination of the witness. And thank you, Mr. President, for helping us communicate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these nice words, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, we must have the second break now, but do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, there are no more questions for you, Witness. The Chamber would like to thank you as well. Thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and assist us to find the truth. You are now, of course, free to return to your normal life, and we wish you all the best for your future life. Thank you very much. The Court Officer will assist you when we -- when the Chamber has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you again. We resume quarter to 6.00, and I think the next witness is then available. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I would like you to remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Please sit down. Mr. Tolimir has still some questions for you. I think -- are we in direct? I was lost. Mr. Vanderpuye, it's your turn. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Witness -- good evening, I should say. When we left off last time, Friday, I was asking you about the sharing of information in the northern facility between the army, the MUP, and I think I mentioned the MUP and the 21st Division in particular. And you indicated that in principle this information was shared amongst you not very often, infrequently. Could you tell us how this information was shared when it was shared.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I assumed this duty, information was not being shared at all. I don't know what the reasons for that were and I didn't inquire. In the first several months of my work there, I felt the need to exchange information. If we had information concerning political leaders which had nothing to do with the army and combat activities, why not convey the information to the persons who were working there. Similarly, if we had information concerning combat activities of primarily the 21st Division, I didn't see why this sort of information could not be shared right there and then and forwarded to the commands concerned. This sort of co-operation intensified in the spring of 1995 with, of course, approval from the command concerned. Ever since that time this exchange of information went smoothly. We provided information to the CSB and vice versa. We also gave information to the 21st Division if we had any, and they would in turn provide us with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the information exchanged electronically? Was it exchanged in hard copy? How was it physically done?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every piece of information in its original form as noted and typed would be conveyed to the CSB. We would merely give our heading and time and say that the information was received from the state security centre, and in this form it would be sent to the command concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P239. I don't think there's any concern about broadcasting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what I'd like to do is I'd like to place side by side in B/C/S -- you know what, I think we maybe shouldn't broadcast it because I want to display also the 2nd Corps intercept, that's 2923A. And I want to see if we can put those side by side without the translation and then we can look at the translation afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my version the document cannot be read at all because the copy I have on my screen is very poor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are in the same position as you, Mr. Tolimir. We are waiting that it comes up on the screen, the other document, and then it should be enlarged, the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, the number is 2923A. All right, I think we do have it on the screen, at least what I'd like to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, could you indicate which portion so that that can be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If we can get it back on the screen. A technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, if we could just focus in on the headers, I think we can start from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the left side you can see that this is a print-out -- I'm sorry, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I can't see a single thing. I can't read the text at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have all the -- perhaps the Court Officer can help to bring it up in a better way and to look at the screen of Mr. Tolimir if that is different from ours. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. The image that Mr. Tolimir can see is much poorer than what the rest of us have here. It must be the fault of the monitor or at any rate the technology on his desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We will do our best to resolve this problem, but I must confess our screen is not much better. It's very poor quality as well. Mr. Vanderpuye, have you a convenient, clear picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I have the advantage of knowing exactly what it says, so to me it's quite clear. But we can take it in stages and I think it will become clear as what I'm using it for, and it's not necessarily for substantive purposes so I don't think there's that much stock to be placed in it. It's only really to demonstrate or to illustrate certain things relevant to the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, were these intercepts part of this binder we got in hard copy recently? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think -- yes, I think the one on the right most definitely was. That was, I think, admitted in the package relevant to PW-024. The one on the left, however, was -- is not part of it and that's the reason why it's on the screen, is I wanted to show you something about it. But I think we can proceed. If you're able to blow up any part of the screen, that's fine. If we can blow up just the top part so we can see the caption on the left and on the right, that would be a good start. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the left side, Witness, you can see that it indicates this is a print-out. It reads Army Republika of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You can see that second -- from the 2nd Corps. Then it indicates the site and the report number, 05/12795. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say I can't see it that well, but I do see. I can manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And is that a report that would be generated by your unit, the one on the left?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as this part above the dotted line is concerned, it's the kind of report that we prepare for transmission, while the part below the dotted line is the report taken over from the CSB SDB, meaning State Security Service, of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to focus you on in particular in this document, if we can go down to the bottom, is you'll see the number 557.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could focus on that particular intercept and maybe we can blow it up. All right. And if we could go and find the match on the other side, the other document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, are you able to see both of these -- both of these notations in these reports, the one on the left and the one on the right, corresponding to report number 557?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And looking at them, can you tell if they're identical?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see, they're absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the nature or the way in which information was exchanged between the MUP and your unit -- CSB, I should say, and your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case we're looking at a report that we got from the SDB, the State Security Service, and sent to the relevant command. We can see that the number of the route covered by them is 557, while this same connecting route has a different reference number given by us. I also see that this was monitored on the radio relay route Zvornik-Vlasenica on the frequency 785.000 megahertz. Since the people who were doing this had no particular military experience, the route Zvornik-Vlasenica never existed as a route. There was a connection from Zvornik to Gucevo in Serbia, or Cer, and then with a different type of communication, SMC 132 Veliki Zep and from then on to Vlasenica, the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before I do, Mr. President, I would like to tender the document on the left, that's 65 ter 2923A. It does not have an English translation. The translation for P239, however, to the extent that it's identical, can serve as a translation for this document as well. But if you'd prefer, I can have a translation made for 2923A separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that would be appreciated because we are -- want to show that the -- there is an identical text, and in that case it should be translated as well. That will be marked for identification, but could you please indicate is there a handwritten B/C/S original document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For this document I believe there is. I'm not tendering it at this point because to the extent that it's attached to a witness that may be coming, I think it would be more appropriate to enter it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received and marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you tender this under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it should be tendered under seal. And Ms. Stewart has pointed out to me if it's possible to mark this exhibit as P239A so that it's connected to the other exhibit that's on the screen, if it's possible. I don't know whether we can do it that way, but otherwise we can just make a record of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I received the information that the document P239 is not under seal. In this case I think it's not necessary to receive this new exhibit under seal. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, the problem is -- I'm sorry. The problem is that with respect to this document it has certain information that is protected in the record that the other document, which is identical in substance to it, doesn't have. So I think you're right, it would be difficult to connect them in any event because one would be under seal and the other one wouldn't be, but it's okay. For the record then, we'll just make a note of the exhibit number and I'll make a record that it's specifically attached to the P239. [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, the Chamber would receive it as a new document with a new number marked for identification under seal. I think this is the most appropriate way to be able to identify and to distinguish between both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 2923A will be Exhibit P268, under seal, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have, please, 65 ter 3113 in e-court, please. I will need 65 ter 311B -- 3113B and I will need also 3113C, and just the B/C/S so that we can place them side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Witness, I have in front of you now on the left-hand side another document. It's headed Army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it has also a report number of 06/21795. Below the caption you can see that this is an intercept between -- it says Puk Cerovich and a general. And you can see on the right-hand side a document that is entitled "CSB SDB Tuzla," and that the caption of it, we'll get a translation but it should read from the PEB counter-electronic warfare of the 2nd Corps. Do you see those documents in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you look at the two intercepts in this case, you can see that substantively they are identical. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the type of information that you would, that is, your unit, would furnish to the CSB or SDB?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is the reverse case. This report received -- was received by my unit. It was captured within the range of the RRU-1 device. It's the usual report when there was no audibility of the speaker at the other end of the line. This report was handed over to the CSB and they sent it, as far as I can see, in its original form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, I'd like to show you -- well, first of all, I'd just like you to make a note of the location from which the 2nd Corps document -- well, make a note of the location that the 2nd Corps document indicates, okay, because I want to show you another document and that is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the site --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please turn off your microphone. Please carry on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the site where it was recorded, it's the northern location, the northern site, where the State Security Service had its listening unit too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is 65 ter 311A [sic], and I'd like to keep the CSB document also on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can't do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps repeat the number to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The number is 65 ter 3113A, and I would like to keep on the screen, if we can, the one on the right, which I believe is 65 ter 3113B. If we can. If not, it's no problem, we can just go to the next document also. And it shouldn't be broadcast also. If we could just blow up the part where you can see it says "1305." All right. That's just -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, Witness, is a notebook entry of an operator attached to the 21st Division. And if you look at the substance of this - we don't have translations in front of us - but if you look at the substance of this intercept, can you tell if it corresponds to the intercept on the right which indicates a time of 1304. If you're not able to see it, just let me know and I can blow it up and perhaps we can even read them both into the record so that it's more clear.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it and I think it's a report written down in a notebook among the reports collected by my unit. It has an indication of frequency, hour, participants in the conversation, and the signature of the person who collected this information. The report is absolutely identical to the one from SDB Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the kind of information that was shared between the SDB, the 21st Division, and your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, since I had already had two years experience in the intelligence-gathering section, it was obvious that the information needed to be collated on the spot for transparency sake and the relevant commander approved it. And it was quite normal to collate information. Every piece of information collected at the level of the division was always interesting to the corps, although the information available to the corps was not always of interest to the division. The information that was of interest was mainly the one that concerned the area of responsibility of the division, namely, the Posavina and the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these are completely different telegrams and the contents are different. For instance, the third sentence says in the manuscript: "It concerns those Talic's men." And in the other transcript it says: "They will go with Talic's men."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was my observation as well. Thank you. That can't be absolutely identical. If you look at the second line, after the capital letter C there is some difference to the text on the left side. You should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just about to. Thank you, Mr. President. What I'd like to show is 65 ter 3113D, as in David, and if we could put that -- it's a notebook entry, if we could place that side by side to the notebook entry that's here.

utterances.text: That means the handwritten notebook on the left side should stay on the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, Mr. President. If we're able to place the 1304 entry somewhere close to the 1305 entry so that we can compare them. All right, that's probably close enough. What we have here are two notebook entries, as you can see, one with a time of 1305, monitoring a frequency of 255.850, and another one with a frequency of 1304 -- I mean, with a time of 1304, with a frequency of 255 -- monitoring 255.850. Both of these intercepts concern a Puk Cerovic and a general. Now, Mr. Tolimir is correct that these intercepts are not absolutely identical --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But looking at the two intercepts, can you tell if they're related to the same subject matter or concern the same event?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it's been 15 years now, I think that these two entries are identical, that the report on the left was captured on the southern location because the name in the signature belongs to a person who was there. And I believe the report on the right was captured by the northern location. It's one of those typical situations when they covered the same frequency without knowing that they were doing the same thing, monitoring the same frequency. I also emphasised earlier that errors are quite possible in the speed that we had to work with. One letter, one sound, can be missed and the computers we had were old. And you can see that every letter that normally should have a diacritic, for instance, C with a diacritic, was typed as CH because that's the only thing we could do on that type of computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender both of these documents. I would -- I think they may have to be marked for identification and I will supply the Trial Chamber with the appropriate English translations -- actually, I think they both have them and I'll identify them for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So it's 65 ter 3113A is the English translation of -- okay, and it has an attached English translation, I understand. Okay. So 65 ter 3113A. And I'd like to tender 65 ter 3113D, under seal.

utterances.text: We have seen a written, a typed transcript of this handwritten version. Do you tender that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, and it's 3113B is the print-out of the handwritten on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have mentioned in terms of the organisation and personnel of the northern and southern facilities that there was -- that there were platoons that were assigned there, platoon commanders, squad commanders, and so on. Did the platoon commanders supervise -- or squad commanders, I should say, supervise the operators that were there on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Squad commanders not only supervised but actively worked on the job for the simple reason that these platoons and squads were never manned to full strength. Some of the personnel had to be dispatched to the front line, and only a minimum number was assigned to such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did the platoon commanders also participate in the interception process and supervise the operators?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The commander was both the soldier, the commander, controller, and everything else. He actively participated in all these activities 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were the squad commanders and platoon commanders, were they responsible for the quality of the work that was done at the interception sites?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, people worked like slaves, as it were, in order that they be kept there rather than sent to the areas of combat. That's why for the duration of their stay at these sites while they were on duty, they did the best to do the job as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did there ever arise an occasion where an operator had to be disciplined for poor conduct or for poor-quality work?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, cautions were always present in our work. As far as I remember, a year before more than 50 per cent of the personnel who were manning the unit were reassigned and sent to the front lines. I'm referring to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that a form of discipline or was that a matter of necessity?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more a matter of necessity, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of the equipment that was made available to the operators in order to do their work, you mentioned that there were notebooks that were provided to them, there were tape recorders that were provided to them. Can you tell us what other kinds of equipment was available or made available to the operators?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every operator tried to make their contribution by bringing in their notebooks. As far as logistics is concerned, the only thing that the command of the 2nd Corps provided in sufficient quantity was food. The rest was down to our resourcefulness. We would be given a number of notebooks, but that was never enough. So we had to resort to our own devices, find all the notepads or notebooks that were used on one side of a sheet. I know that a truck-load of such paper was brought to us. Other stationery that was supposed to be destroyed was not, there were delays, and we would be provided with that, as well as with cigarette paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 01357 in e-court, please, to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's on the screen in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here is a radio amateur equipment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that's the set to the left. Whereas the device to the right is ICER-100. I'm not sure, though, it's been a long time. These devices were brought to us from radio clubs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the device to the right, can you tell us what that does, if you know. What is its function?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one on the right can play a dual role. It may be difficult to explain to the Chamber. One of the options is that it can receive short waves, and the second, to analyse signals from RRU-800 radio lengths.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the device on the right, it says "Kenwood" on there, if you can see that, what does that do?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, these devices were used to expand the range and to receive signals emitted from RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in their original form were they able to do that or did they need to be modified by the operators or other people working in the unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To explain this I need to say a few technical things. This device was possible to receive one -- to capture one channel or one frequency, and that's one of the ways in which the signal from RRU-800 could be received. In order to improve the quality of the signal, an attachment, that's to say an amplifier, was added to this device in order to make the signal audible. There was another device that was also the product of our mechanics, which is the converter - it was a makeshift device - and its role was as follows. Since these were not military devices and were not produced for professional use, whichever signal you wanted to capture it didn't have a fixed frequency. And the converter had the role of placing, fixing, the signal at 16 or 18 megahertz which is where -- the fixed frequencies that we had. I don't know if I can explain this. The device was not calibrated to receive military frequencies. It was not fixed onto military frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did it have to be modified in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The first task that we had was to expand the range. Since these sets were mostly intended for ultra -- rather, for short-wave ranges. Even though some may gainsay what I said just now, it is true that these devices could be used to bridge this difficulty. There were four ways of doing it. The first one was to use this device - and we did this, as you will see in the reports - to cover one frequency and one channel. One transmitting and one receiving frequency. If you have two speakers, what is the receiving signal to one side will be the transmitting signal to the other side. So this was a way of monitoring both the receiving and the transmitting end at different channels, but it was difficult to fit these conversations together. We didn't have the technical options for that. The second way that was also used frequently was to follow one frequency, be it the transmitting or the receiving one, and because of two anomalies or imperfections of the device itself, we would follow both speakers. These anomalies consist of the following. The first one: Because of the feedback, you see we have the telephone and, of course, the role of the microphone and the role of the receiver is similar. So the speaker speaking into the phone on the other end, his voice would be transmitted through the receiver and that's how we would hear what the other speaker at the other end was saying. That was one of the technical possibilities we used. The other anomaly is the following. Because it was impossible to have differential sets in the devices at the terminal stations and because we had to pass from four-wire systems to two-wire systems - and this was a specific system used by the army - we got the maximum out of what we had. The same applies to RRU-800 and to RRU-1. A moment ago we were able to see the frequency from the RRU-1 range, where this return signal was quite audible. We had another speaker speaking -- or rather, we had two speakers, speaker one and speaker two, speaking on one frequency. This is a classic example of a telephone situation, where the telephone doesn't work properly, and for that very reason we were able to hear the other speaker. Although, normally the voice of the other speaker should be carried either 10 megahertz higher or 10 megahertz lower than the frequency on which the speaker at this end was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I just want to ask you a little bit about the antenna systems that you had available at the respective northern and southern sites. Just generally and really in very -- the most plain and basic terms, can you tell us what types of antennas you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it simply, 90 per cent of antennae were handmade, makeshift antennae, done out of traffic signs, water pipelines, copper wires with built-in amplifiers. I recall that we had one military parabolic antenna as well. We used old television antennas, which proved to work quite well on certain frequencies. In other words, we didn't have specifically the antennae we needed. That's to say, we had this -- we had several of the military parabolic antenna and the rest were makeshift antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to show you 65 ter 1632.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before I do, Ms. Stewart has reminded me, I'd like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P270.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us -- first of all, are these the kinds of antennas that you've described?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. But in 1995, the mast that we can see here did not exist. The antennae were placed on roof-tops. To the left we can see a parabolic antenna, which was the military antenna I was referring to; the one in the middle is a helicoidal antenna; and the other two are Yagi antennae. We also see a stick antenna, which is the rod in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to offer these -- I'm sorry, this photo into evidence. I have two others which also depict the same or similar antennas. They are 1633 and 1634, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And do you want to have them as one exhibit, the three photos? No, as separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They can go in together, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm told it's better for clear identification to have them separate. They will all three be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1632 will be Exhibit P271. 65 ter 1633 will be Exhibit P272. 65 ter 1634 will be Exhibit P272 -- 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to recognise the location where these antennas are?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to this photograph, it's at the northern site.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you 65 ter 1635. Now, this appears to be another parabolic antenna. Can you identify for us where -- the location of this site?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I can see, I think the antenna was located at the southern site, on the roof of the southern site.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to move this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 65 ter 1635. There is also 65 ter 1636, 1637, and 1638. I'd like to show the witness the last one, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They all four will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1635 will be Exhibit P274. 65 ter 1636 will be Exhibit P275. 65 ter 1637 will be Exhibit P276. 65 ter 1638 will be Exhibit P277.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to show you this particular antenna and I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about it.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a makeshift helicoidal antenna. Such antennae that we made could not pick up all of the range used by RRU-800. So we had to make several antennae which would cover 650 to 700 frequencies, or 750 to 800, or 850 to 900. What does it mean that it resonates at a certain frequency? It means that it works best in terms of resonance activity and capture. You can see that this was a makeshift antenna. The pipe that you see is the sewage pipe. The antenna has a pre-amplifier and twists of copper wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, you were asked a few questions, I think, concerning how it was that VRS communications were able to be intercepted given the fact that they knew or should have known they were being listened to. I would like to show you 65 ter 2978 in relation to that evidence that you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand it's 2978A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can all see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we can blow up the translation a little bit so that everybody can see that more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an intercept that was taken by an operator in the 2nd Corps, and it concerns a conversation between Panorama 3 and a Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. And in that conversation you can see, as it reads -- it starts off with C, who says: "And who wants to know?" Panorama 3 responds: "Panorama 3." C says: "Panorama B?" P says: "Panorama 3." And C says: "Aha, you need Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, right?" And you can see the response where P calls him a stupid idiot. And then if you look further down you can see that this happens again. I think in the B/C/S you'll find that on the second page, and in the English you'll find that just underneath where it says: "All right, you're talking fast, man ..." And if you read further down you see where it says: "Slow down, slow down, don't talk too much. You should know better and tell that idiot next time not to mention any names, ranks, or last names." And then if you look further down, you can see where P says: "You're worse than the one who put me through to you. He says the rank, the name, the last name ... the only thing missing was the date of birth, the current location and what his intentions are. You read him the riot act and teach him not to ask who's calling when a person gives his code name. The name is Panorama. You don't ask any additional questions." And this, as you can see in this intercept, is this the kind of thing that you would see when you reviewed the intercepts in terms of how VRS officers, VRS personnel acted in relation to securing their radio communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can mention some of the features of these report. There are some characteristics in the way this conversation took place. Initially they would ask for the call signal, they would ask to be switched to someone else, and that's what I meant when I was referring to them transferring from a four-wire communication to a two-wire communication. We have a channel where both speakers participate. So technically speaking, we can hear both interlocutors. Now, as for the context of this conversation and failure to meet the rules of confidentiality, all the units and armies had code-names. If the code-name is Panorama, then the commander would be Panorama 1. The commanding officers had tables of codes for identification. They would say, "Can I speak to Panorama 325." Normally these codes would change every ten days or so. A third feature from this report is the failure to abide by these rules, having a big mouth, talking -- saying too much. As we can see in this case it was the operator, but sometimes it so happened that the commanders would do that. It is beyond doubt that the VRS had protected channels, ones that we could not intercept. These communication lines went from the VRS Main Staff to Belgrade and to subordinate corps. We could not intercept the communications taking place along SMC-130. That's true as well. And of course what we saw before was the extent of what we could intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see that it's time. I'd like to tender this into evidence. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asked if that have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, it don't have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, could you indicate how long your examination-in-chief will last tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have a signal here that I have used up three hours and 20 minutes. I think I can wrap it up in about the remaining time, which is another 40 minutes. The reason is I have two areas, two significant areas I'd like to cover with the witness. One has to do with chain of custody, which hopefully will go quickly; and another one has to do with explaining a war-time map and the way the radio communications were intercepted.
